previous.passage: What do you do with praise in a language you barely own? After I won the provincial recitation prize in Indonesian, my grandfather Wira's back room in Chengdu filled with cousins who wanted me to talk to them, and I could only repeat my speech. Wira said little. He went on marking cloth with his flat blue chalk, drawing lines he would cut along and then brush away. When I asked why he never kept the marks, he said a coat should not remember how it was measured. That week he stopped correcting my grammar in front of the cousins. Instead he left chalk words on the cutting table each morning, two or three, faint as breath. I copied them into my notebook before he wiped the table clean. By winter the notebook was thicker than my prize certificate, and I, Zihan, kept it in the drawer with his pins.
previous.question: In the text, Wira's chalk marks most likely represent

previous.passage: Still keeping my shuttle, I see, Lucien said, before he had even taken off his coat. Imtiaz did not look up from the warp. For eleven years she had rented the corner room of the Lyon cooperative from him, and for nine of those years his walnut shuttle had passed through her cloth, darker now from the oil of her hands. He had lent it the winter her own split, a loan, he said at the time, until the new one comes. The new one had come and gone into a drawer. Lucien crossed to the window and looked at the bolts stacked there, blue and rust and grey, each carrying the same faint line where the walnut caught the thread. By now, he said, the thing has put down roots in your loom. Imtiaz threw the shuttle once more and let it rest in the shed. Lucien buttoned his coat again and asked about the rent for spring.
previous.question: As used in the text, the phrase “put down roots in your loom” most nearly suggests that the shuttle
options: has become so bound up with Imtiaz's work that reclaiming it no longer seems right.
has been worn by long use until it can no longer be pulled free of the loom.
has been hidden by Imtiaz so that Lucien will forget that he ever owned it.

previous.explanation: 북은 9년 동안 Imtiaz의 천을 지나며 손때로 검어졌고, 그녀가 짠 모든 천에 같은 흔적을 남겼다. Lucien은 돌려 달라고 말을 꺼냈지만 천을 본 뒤 이 표현을 쓰고는 코트를 다시 잠그며 화제를 바꾼다. 따라서 이 구절은 북이 그녀의 작업과 하나가 되어 되찾는 것이 더 이상 옳지 않게 느껴진다는 뜻이므로 A가 정답이다. B는 비유를 문자 그대로 읽었고, C는 숨김이라는 근거 없는 의도를 덧붙였으며, D는 Lucien의 태도 변화의 방향을 뒤집은 오답이다.

previous.passage: Gymnasiums keep every sound. Caoimhe noticed that as she waited on the bench in the Glasgow school gym beside Jianguo while the deputy head read out the janitor's statement: the boy had been seen near the equipment cupboard at four, and the door had been forced at ten past. Jianguo kept bouncing a ball he had picked up, a slow, insolent rhythm. Caoimhe asked the deputy, crisply, whether the janitor's watch had been checked, whether anyone else had a key, whether the cupboard lock was already broken. She sounded, she knew, like a solicitor. Then the deputy mentioned that Jianguo's PE teacher remembered him in the library until half four, helping a first-year with fractions. The ball stopped. Caoimhe looked at him, and he looked at the floor, and she realized she had never once heard him mention helping anyone. She put her hand flat on the bench between them, not quite touching his.

previous.passage: Bologna in March meant mud on the kitchen tiles, and Elisa, who had owned the boarding house for nine days, was cataloguing it. She listed the cracked cups, the broken latch, the account book with two years torn out. Rania, the gardener, stood by the door with her boots off and answered each question in the same flat way: she did not know, she could not say, the previous owner had handled that. Elisa underlined the missing years twice. Then, looking for a pen, she opened the drawer under the sink and found a child's school report tucked behind the dishcloths, the name on it the old owner's grandson, the address this house. She looked up. Rania was watching the report, not her. Elisa slid it back beneath the cloths and closed the drawer gently, and when she spoke again she asked only whether the fig tree needed pruning before the rains.

previous.passage: When Renata moved to Arequipa, I kept her key to our bookbinding workshop in Lima on a nail above my bench and told everyone it was simply easier that way. For a year our messages were cheerful and brief: photographs of glue pots, jokes about clients who wanted leather on everything. Then the June storm flooded the back room, and while I was hauling out soaked boards I found the box she had hidden under the floor slats: a dozen blank journals she had bound for me, one for each month she would be gone, the first inscribed Ximena and dated the week she left. I sat on the wet floor with them. The jokes I had been sending her seemed suddenly thin, a way of not asking. That night I did not write anything funny. I asked her how she was, and then I waited, and I let the waiting be uncomfortable.

previous.passage: Once a year, on the date of our first concert, Yitzhak and I swam at the old salt-water pool in Thessaloniki, and the tenth year was supposed to be no different. I arrived with a list. We could book the harbor hall, I told him in the changing room; we could rearrange the early songs, invite the critic who had liked us once. Then he said my name, Eleni, and told me quietly that his hands had been shaking on the frets since spring. I stopped swimming. We hung on the rope at the deep end, neither of us mentioning the hall again, the salt stinging our eyes, and I watched a gull work at something on the empty diving board.

previous.passage: Tehran in late October is mild enough to sit outside, so my brother Bahram and I read our mother's letters on the bench by the cemetery gate rather than in the empty house. We had sold the carpets, given the books to the mosque library, and left only the brass samovar, which neither of us would claim. In the letters, written to her sister over thirty years, the samovar appears again and again: polished for Nowruz, dented in a move, mended by a man who charged too much. __I had always believed she kept it only because it was too heavy to give away.__ Bahram read one passage aloud twice, in which she wrote that the samovar was the first thing she unpacked in every new home, before the beds. Neither of us spoke for a while. Then he folded the letter, slid it back into its envelope, and said he would bring the car around, since the samovar would fit in the back if we laid it on a blanket.
